wave_family: reflected: bulk plane P wave incident on the free plane boundary of a half-space, producing three reflected fractional waves (thermal T, longitudinal p, shear SV)
constitutive_model: generalized thermoelasticity with three-phase-lag (TPL) heat conduction written with a conformable fractional derivative; initial stress; temperature-dependent elastic modulus
geometry: half-space with a plane free surface; two-dimensional reduction with displacement components in the surface plane and zero out-of-plane displacement; incidence and reflection angles measured from the surface normal (Fig. 1 puts the incident wave at an angle with the negative z-axis). The text also calls the region a quarter-space and states that the field functions are independent of z, while the traction conditions are written for quantities evaluated at (x,0,t), so the surface coordinate is named inconsistently
couplings: thermo-mechanical: elastic dilatation coupled to temperature; initial stress P in the momentum equation; temperature-dependent modulus f(T) = f0 (1 + a (T - T0)) with empirical constant a; fractional-order heat conduction
assumptions: homogeneous isotropic crust material; small-displacement linear theory; plane strain with zero out-of-plane displacement; vacuum above the free surface, no radiation back into the medium; incidence angle swept from 0 to 90 deg
governing_formulation: momentum and energy equations in TPL form with conformable fractional derivatives (Eqs. (1)-(25)); displacement potentials for the coupled T, p and SV waves; harmonic wave solutions with Snell law (45); traction-free and thermally insulated surface conditions (46)-(50); the algebraic system (46) with (48)-(50) for p-incidence yields the amplitude ratios Z1, Z2, Z3
verification: no independent validation: the fractional-order results are only compared with the integer-order case, and the authors state that the method agrees with the integer derivative when the fractional parameter equals one; no experimental data and no published numerical benchmark are compared
parameters_and_units: Crust (Table 1): CE = 1100 J/(kg K); mu = 3e10 N/m2; rho = 2900 kg/m3; g = 9.8; T0 = 300 K (the remaining table entries print with garbled digits or units and are not recorded); fractional parameter 0.90, 0.94, 0.98 and 1; empirical material constant a = 0.011, 0.012, 0.013, 0.014; initial stress P = 1, 2, 3 x 1e14; heat-gradient lag tau_T = 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 1.2; heat-flux lag tau_q = 0.85, 0.90, 0.95, 1
reported_result: for p-incidence the magnitude of Z1 starts from its maximum at 0 deg and tends to unity at 90 deg, Z2 falls with incidence angle and vanishes at 90 deg, and Z3 rises from zero, peaks at a small incidence angle (the printed digit is ambiguous) and returns to zero at 90 deg (Fig. 2); raising the initial stress lowers Z1 and Z3 but raises Z2, whereas raising a raises Z1 and Z3 and lowers Z2, so P and a act oppositely (Figs. 3-4); increasing tau_T lowers Z1 while Z2 grows, and increasing tau_q slightly raises Z1 and Z3 while strongly lowering Z2 (Figs. 5-6); the integer-order case gives the largest magnitudes (conclusion 2)
limitations: graphical results only, no tabulated values; no experimental or independent numerical validation; several Table 1 entries illegible in the text layer; surface coordinate named inconsistently (z-axis wording, quarter-space, quantities as functions of (x,0,t)); signs and subscripts of the amplitude equations are not recoverable from the text layer
sources: AboDahab S.M., Kilany A.A., Abdel-Salam E.A.-B., Hatem A. (2020) Results in Physics 18:103270; DOI 10.1016/j.rinp.2020.103270; PDF 1-s2.0-S221137972031737X-main.pdf
reproducibility: complete analytical derivation with numbered equations and boundary conditions; material constants given in Table 1 (partly illegible); no code, no numerical algorithm and no tabulated data reported, so the figures cannot be regenerated from the paper alone

wave_family: reflected: bulk plane SV wave incident on the free plane boundary of a half-space, producing three reflected fractional waves (thermal T, longitudinal p, shear SV)
constitutive_model: generalized thermoelasticity with three-phase-lag (TPL) heat conduction written with a conformable fractional derivative; initial stress; temperature-dependent elastic modulus
geometry: same half-space and free plane surface as P5-101, with the incident wave taken as a shear vertical wave; the incidence angle is measured from the surface normal and the field is stated to be independent of the third coordinate (two-dimensional reduction), while the boundary conditions (47)-(50) are written for quantities evaluated at (x,0,t)
couplings: thermo-mechanical coupling; initial stress P; temperature-dependent modulus through the empirical constant a; fractional-order heat conduction
assumptions: homogeneous isotropic crust material; small-displacement linear theory; plane strain with zero out-of-plane displacement; vacuum above the free surface; incidence angle swept from 0 to 90 deg
governing_formulation: same governing equations as P5-101 (Eqs. (1)-(25)); for SV-incidence the surface conditions (47)-(50) together with Snell law (45) give the algebraic system whose solution is the set of amplitude ratios Z1, Z2, Z3
verification: no independent validation: only the integer-order case is compared with the fractional-order results (authors state agreement when the fractional parameter equals one); no experiment and no published numerical benchmark
parameters_and_units: Crust (Table 1): CE = 1100 J/(kg K); mu = 3e10 N/m2; rho = 2900 kg/m3; g = 9.8; T0 = 300 K (other entries illegible); fractional parameter 0.90, 0.94, 0.98 and 1; a = 0.011-0.014; initial stress P = 1, 2, 3 x 1e14; tau_T = 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 1.2; tau_q = 0.85, 0.90, 0.95, 1
reported_result: for SV-incidence Z1 falls and Z2 rises as the initial stress increases, while Z3 rises slightly below 45 deg, peaks at 45 deg and then falls (Fig. 7); increasing a lowers Z1 and Z2 and leaves Z3 unchanged (Fig. 8); approaching the integer order lowers Z1 and Z2 but leaves Z3 unchanged (Fig. 9); increasing tau_T lowers Z1 and Z2 and leaves Z3 unchanged (Fig. 10); the heat-flux lag affects only Z2 (Fig. 11)
limitations: graphical results only, no tabulated values; no experimental or independent numerical validation; Table 1 partly illegible; boundary coordinate naming inconsistent; amplitude equation signs not recoverable from the text layer
sources: AboDahab S.M., Kilany A.A., Abdel-Salam E.A.-B., Hatem A. (2020) Results in Physics 18:103270; DOI 10.1016/j.rinp.2020.103270; PDF 1-s2.0-S221137972031737X-main.pdf
reproducibility: complete analytical derivation with numbered equations and boundary conditions; no code, no numerical algorithm and no tabulated data reported

wave_family: reflected: bulk plane qP and qSV waves at the free plane boundary of a half-space; both waves are dispersive because of strain gradient and micro-inertia
constitutive_model: flexoelectric dielectric with strain-gradient elasticity, micro-inertia and static bulk flexoelectric coupling (isotropic single crystal)
geometry: half-space x3 >= 0 with free plane boundary x3 = 0; x1 along the boundary and x3 the depth; plane strain in the x1-x3 plane; incidence angle theta0 measured from the x3 axis (Fig. 1)
couplings: electro-mechanical flexoelectric coupling; strain-gradient (non-uniform strain) elastic coupling; micro-inertia
assumptions: homogeneous isotropic SrTiO3 single crystal; infinitesimal deformation; traction-free boundary; electrically open (charge-free) boundary; no body force; no attenuation
governing_formulation: two-dimensional equations of motion with strain-gradient and micro-inertia terms (1)-(4); Gauss equation for the electric displacement; plane-wave ansatz leading to the two coupled velocity equations (11)-(12); Snell law (17); free and electrically open boundary conditions (14)-(16); reflection coefficients (18); energy ratios (19)-(21)
verification: energy check only: the sum of the energy ratios of the reflected waves is observed to be at most one in the plotted ranges, and the paper claims qualitative agreement with Qi (2019); no numerical benchmark, grid study or experimental comparison is reported
parameters_and_units: SrTiO3: eps0 = 8.85e-12 F/m; d12 = 1.16 GPa; d44 = 0.52 GPa; rho0 = 4810 kg/m3; f = 5.65e6 N m2/C2 (flexocoupling); a12 = a44 = a77 = 1.38e-6 N m4/C2; length scale l = 1, 5 and 10 nm; dimensionless wavenumber kl, micro-inertia ratio n/l and f varied; propagation angle theta0 = 45 deg for the speed plots; incidence angle swept 0 to 90 deg for qP incidence
reported_result: qP and qSV speeds are dispersive: at small wavenumber both speeds coincide for all n/l, the speeds fall as the micro-inertial factor rises and as the static bulk flexoelectric coefficient rises, and with n = 0 the strain gradient makes both waves faster (Figs. 2-4 and conclusion i); the reflection coefficients of the reflected qP and qSV waves change with kl, n/l and f, and the largest drop in the reflected qP coefficient occurs near 65 deg for strain gradient and near 64 deg for flexoelectricity (Figs. 5-7); the qSV energy ratio is zero at 0 deg and peaks at 64.1, 66.1 and 69.1 deg for the three kl values, the dispersion effect on energy shares being concentrated between 60 and 70 deg (Figs. 8-10)
limitations: isotropic single-crystal model; no damping; results are graphs only; the claimed agreement with Qi (2019) is qualitative and not quantified; no experimental data
sources: Singh B., Gupta G. (2020) Mechanics Based Design of Structures and Machines; DOI 10.1080/15397734.2020.1853566; PDF B05-020__Singh, Gupta - 2023 - Wave reflection by the fr.pdf
reproducibility: complete derivation with numbered equations, boundary conditions and material constants; a MATLAB program is said to have been used for the velocity equation but no code and no tabulated data are supplied

wave_family: reflected: bulk plane qSV wave incident on the free plane boundary of a half-space, with a critical incidence angle beyond which the reflected qP wave disappears
constitutive_model: flexoelectric dielectric with strain-gradient elasticity, micro-inertia and static bulk flexoelectric coupling (isotropic single crystal)
geometry: same half-space x3 >= 0 with free boundary x3 = 0 and plane strain in x1-x3; the incidence angle theta0 of the qSV wave is restricted to 0 to 28 deg because the reflected qP wave does not exist beyond that angle (Fig. 11)
couplings: electro-mechanical flexoelectric coupling; strain-gradient elastic coupling; micro-inertia
assumptions: homogeneous isotropic SrTiO3 single crystal; infinitesimal deformation; traction-free and electrically open boundary; incidence restricted to 0-28 deg (subcritical range only)
governing_formulation: same formulation as P5-103 (Eqs. (1)-(18)); for qSV incidence the reflected amplitudes A1/B0 and A2/B0 follow from the same algebraic system, evaluated only over the subcritical range 0 to 28 deg; energy ratios E1 and E2 as in (19)-(21)
verification: energy check only: the sum of energy ratios of the reflected waves is plotted and remains at most one in the subcritical range; no experiment and no independent numerical benchmark
parameters_and_units: SrTiO3: eps0 = 8.85e-12 F/m; d12 = 1.16 GPa; d44 = 0.52 GPa; rho0 = 4810 kg/m3; f = 5.65e6 N m2/C2; a12 = a44 = a77 = 1.38e-6 N m4/C2; l = 1, 5 and 10 nm; kl, n/l and f varied; theta0 from 0 to 28 deg
reported_result: for qSV incidence the reflected qP wave does not exist beyond theta0 = 28 deg, so coefficients and energy shares are evaluated from 0 to 28 deg (Sec. 5.2(b), Fig. 11); the reflected qP coefficient grows monotonically with theta0 while the qSV coefficient falls to a minimum at 26.1 deg and then rises; kl, n/l and f hardly change these coefficients in the subcritical range; the energy ratios E1 and E2 are plotted for the same range (Fig. 12)
limitations: subcritical range only, so nothing is reported about the post-critical field; results are graphs only; no experimental data; conclusion item (iii) attaches the 28 deg limit to the reflected qSV wave while Sec. 5.2(b) attaches it to the reflected qP wave
sources: Singh B., Gupta G. (2020) Mechanics Based Design of Structures and Machines; DOI 10.1080/15397734.2020.1853566; PDF B05-020__Singh, Gupta - 2023 - Wave reflection by the fr.pdf
reproducibility: complete derivation and material constants reported; no code and no tabulated data supplied

wave_family: reflected: bulk plane P wave (hygrothermal) incident on the free surface of a half-space, producing four reflected waves (P, thermal diffusion TD, moisture diffusion mD, SV)
constitutive_model: Eringen nonlocal hygro-thermoelasticity with coupled heat conduction and moisture diffusion in a non-dissipative medium
geometry: half-space z >= 0 with the origin on the stress-free plane surface z = 0, propagation in the x-z plane, incidence angle theta0 measured from the surface normal and fixed at 45 deg in the numerical results (Fig. 1). The potentials (53)-(54) write the depth coordinate as y while the boundary conditions (55) use z, so the depth coordinate is not named consistently
couplings: thermo-mechanical coupling (thermal expansion); hygro-mechanical coupling (moisture expansion); heat-moisture diffusion coupling; nonlocal stress-strain coupling through the nonlocal parameter f, which also enters the stress boundary conditions as the operator (1 - f2 grad2)
assumptions: homogeneous isotropic medium; small deformation; non-dissipative medium so the energy ratios sum to one at the interface; free surface thermally insulated and moisture impermeable as written in (55), although the text also mentions an isothermal option; no body force
governing_formulation: nonlocal constitutive relations with hygro-thermal strains; moisture flux by Fick law; coupled heat and moisture diffusion equations; displacement potentials and the plane-wave ansatz (53)-(54); dispersion relations (51)-(52) giving three roots plus the SV root; Snell law (56); boundary conditions (55); the 4x4 non-homogeneous system (57) for the four reflected amplitudes; energy ratios from the surface power (58)
verification: energy conservation check only: the sum of the energy ratios of the four reflected waves is stated to remain one as the incidence angle varies from 0 to 90 deg (conclusion 5); no experimental data and no comparison with a published numerical solution
parameters_and_units: k = 46.92e9 N/m2; mu = 24.17e9 N/m2; rho = 370 kg/m3; alpha_T = 31.3e-6 per degC; alpha_m = 2.68e-3 per percent H2O; m0 = 10.0 percent; C = 2500 J/(kg degC); T0 = 283 K in the constant list but 286 K in the figure captions; Dm = 2.16e-6 m2/s; omega = 30 Hz in the constant list and 5, 10, 15 Hz (also 2, 6, 10 Hz) in the figures; nu = 0.33; l = 1; f = 0.03 by default, swept 0 to 0.3; Dm swept 0.15 to 1.0; theta0 = 45 deg
reported_result: the four reflected waves are P, TD, mD and SV; the nonlocal parameter f changes the reflection coefficients and energy ratios as f goes from 0 to 0.3 at omega = 5, 10 and 15 Hz (Figs. 2-3); the velocities of all four waves rise with frequency and fall as the moisture diffusion parameter rises from 0.15 to 1.0 (conclusions 2 and 4); P, TD and mD are described as highly dispersive and highly attenuating while SV is dispersive (conclusion 3); the sum of the energy ratios remains one for incidence angles from 0 to 90 deg (conclusion 5)
limitations: graphical results only; the temperature used in the figures (286 K) differs from the constant list (283 K); the computation is described only as a FORTRAN program that is not reported; no experimental validation; depth coordinate named inconsistently between the potentials and the boundary conditions
sources: Yadav A.K., Carrera E., Marin M., Othman M.I.A. (2022) Mechanics of Advanced Materials and Structures; DOI 10.1080/15376494.2022.2130484; PDF B03-003__23 PI- 13 MAMS Reflection hygrothermal Nonlocal.pdf
reproducibility: full derivation with numbered equations, boundary conditions and material constants reported; the FORTRAN program mentioned by the authors is not included and no tabulated values are given

wave_family: half-space wave field: two-dimensional normal-mode field varying harmonically along the boundary and decaying into the half-space; not an incidence and reflection problem
constitutive_model: fractional-order (Caputo) generalized thermoelasticity with one relaxation time in a fiber-reinforced medium, with magnetic field and gravity
geometry: half-space x >= 0 bounded by the plane x = 0, two-dimensional field in x and y with fibers along x; the field varies as exp(i b y) along the boundary, where b is the wavenumber in the y direction, and the solution is required to be bounded as x tends to infinity
couplings: thermo-mechanical coupling; fiber-reinforced anisotropy (separate longitudinal and transverse Lame-type constants); Lorentz force from a magnetic field along z; gravity; moving internal heat source
assumptions: homogeneous fiber-reinforced elastic medium; small deformation; normal-mode form with a complex time constant; the medium is unbounded along y; solution bounded as x tends to infinity; single relaxation time
governing_formulation: momentum equations with Lorentz force and gravity (Eqs. (1)-(20)); fractional heat conduction with one relaxation time; normal-mode reduction (23)-(27) to ordinary differential equations (28)-(30); elimination gives the sixth-order equation (31) with characteristic equation (36) and three roots; stress and temperature boundary conditions (63)-(65) on x = 0; amplitudes M1 to M3 from the linear system (66)-(68)
verification: no validation: the figures only compare the field distributions with and without the magnetic field, gravity and heat source and for three fractional orders; no limit reduction, published comparison or experimental check is reported
parameters_and_units: material not named; elastic-type constants 7.59e9, 1.89e10, 2.45e10, -1.28e11 and 0.32e10 N/m2 (symbols render ambiguously in the text layer); rho = 7800 kg/m3; CE = 383.1 J/(kg K); alpha_t = 1.78e-4 1/K; 9.86e11 (symbol ambiguous); kappa = 386 W/(m K); beta = 1.3; g = 9.8 m/s2; tau0 = 0.5; omega = -0.4 + 1.2i; Q0 = 10; t0 = 3; P* = 0.3; y = 0.1; t = 0.1; fractional order 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0
reported_result: distributions of the displacement components u and v, the temperature and the stresses sigma_xx, sigma_xy and sigma_yy against x over 0 to 1.0 at y = 0.1 and t = 0.1 (Figs. 1-21); the presence of the magnetic field, of gravity and of the heat source each changes the profiles, and the three fractional orders give distinguishable curves; no wave speed, dispersion relation or reflection coefficient is reported
limitations: no wave amplitude or speed analysis and no reflection geometry; material unnamed and several constants symbol-ambiguous; only graphical output; the physical meaning of the complex time constant is not discussed
sources: Ma Y., Duan X. (2020) Mechanics Based Design of Structures and Machines; DOI 10.1080/15397734.2020.1852088; PDF 10.1080@15397734.2020.1852088.pdf
reproducibility: derivation and boundary conditions reported with numbered equations and a constant list; no code and no tabulated data included

wave_family: bulk plane waves in a half-space: normal-mode field exp(i a (x - c t)) propagating along x with depth dependence exp(-k z); four wave modes from an eighth-order depth equation; the surface is driven by a prescribed harmonic normal stress
constitutive_model: generalized piezo-thermoelasticity with memory-dependent derivatives under the Lord-Shulman, dual-phase-lag and three-phase-lag heat conduction theories (hexagonal 6 mm piezoelectric medium)
geometry: semi-infinite medium occupying z >= 0 with the boundary at z = 0; solutions are required to be bounded as z tends to infinity (Eq. (36)), which fixes the half-space; the paper itself does not use the word half-space; two-dimensional field in x and z with displacement components u and w
couplings: piezo-thermo-mechanical coupling: elastic, thermal and electric fields are coupled through the piezoelectric constants and the pyroelectric and thermal-expansion coefficients; heat conduction carries the memory-dependent derivative with a chosen kernel function
assumptions: homogeneous hexagonal 6 mm piezoelectric crystal (CdSe); small deformation; linear theory; the surface is loaded by a prescribed harmonic normal stress; the temperature and the normal gradient of the electric potential vanish on the surface; the three heat-conduction theories are compared under the same constants
governing_formulation: non-dimensional field equations (19)-(27); normal-mode decomposition (28) with c = omega/a; the reduced equations (29)-(32) eliminate to the eighth-order depth equation (33)-(34); its four roots (35) give the bounded solutions (36)-(39); boundary conditions (45) at z = 0, namely a prescribed harmonic sigma_zz, zero sigma_xz, zero temperature and zero normal derivative of the electric potential; the resulting system (46)-(50) fixes the amplitudes
verification: model-reduction checks only: setting the conductivity-rate term to zero recovers the dual-phase-lag heat equation, and setting it to zero with tau_q = tau_theta and the fractional parameter zero recovers the Lord-Shulman heat equation; the authors also note that all field variables satisfy the boundary conditions and decay with depth; no numerical, experimental or published-solution comparison is reported
reported_result: distributions of the vertical displacement w, temperature T, stresses sigma_xx and sigma_zz, electric potential and electric displacement Dz against depth z (Figs. 1-18): magnitudes of all field variables decrease with z and the temperature vanishes at z = 0 as required by the boundary conditions (Figs. 1-6); the presence of memory gives smaller magnitudes than no memory, and the choice of kernel function changes the profiles (case I); the delay time has an increasing effect on all distributions (case II, Figs. 7-12, three-phase-lag only); the three theories LS, DPL and TPL give distinguishable curves with and without memory, the largest magnitudes being reported for the Lord-Shulman model (case III, Figs. 13-18)
limitations: graphical results only, no tabulated values; validation is limited to model reductions and to the observation that the profiles satisfy the boundary conditions; the surface load is prescribed rather than free, so no free-surface dispersion relation is obtained; no experimental data
sources: Mondal S., Othman M.I.A. (2020) Waves in Random and Complex Media; DOI 10.1080/17455030.2020.1730480; PDF Piezo-thermoelastic media.pdf
reproducibility: complete derivation with numbered equations and a full CdSe constant list; the coefficients of the depth equation are relegated to supplementary appendices; no code and no tabulated data reported
